# SnakeWise

> SnakeWise is a free, original educational website about snakes for curious beginners and enthusiasts. It explains snake anatomy, movement, venom and constriction, notable species, habitats, common myths, safety around wild snakes and pet snake basics, and offers a region-by-region guide to telling venomous snakes from harmless lookalikes.

The content is general education, not medical advice or a field identification key.

## Guides
- [Snake anatomy](https://snakewise.org/anatomy.html): skeleton, scales and shedding, senses, jaws and organs
- [How snakes move](https://snakewise.org/movement.html): lateral undulation, concertina, rectilinear, sidewinding and gliding; section anchors (#lateral-undulation, #concertina, #rectilinear, #sidewinding, #specialists) and a 6-question FAQ (#faq)
- [Venom vs constriction](https://snakewise.org/venom-constriction.html): how snakes subdue prey, fang types, venomous vs poisonous
- [Snake species facts](https://snakewise.org/species.html): longest, heaviest, smallest and most venomous snakes; comparison table, 12 species profiles with anchors (#king-cobra, #reticulated-python, #inland-taipan, #barbados-threadsnake...) and a 7-question FAQ
- [Where do snakes live? Snake habitats](https://snakewise.org/habitats.html): where snakes live, from rainforests and deserts to oceans and cold climates; section anchors (#distribution, #rainforests, #deserts, #grasslands, #wetlands, #oceans, #cold-climates) and a 6-question FAQ (#faq)
- [Snake myths vs facts](https://snakewise.org/myths.html): 9 common misconceptions corrected, one question per section (are snakes slimy, do they chase people, head-shape ID, first-aid myths)
- [Safety around wild snakes](https://snakewise.org/safety.html): prevention, encounters and snakebite first-aid do's and don'ts
- [Pet snakes for beginners](https://snakewise.org/pets.html): is a snake right for you, best beginner species, enclosure, heat and humidity, what pet snakes eat, and signs of illness (FAQ)
- [Snake glossary](https://snakewise.org/glossary.html): plain-English definitions of 18 snake and herpetology terms (brumation, colubrid, constriction, ecdysis, ectotherm, elapid, fang, heat pit, Jacobson's organ, neurotoxin, oviparous, viviparous, ophiophagous, scute, spectacle/brille, venom, viper and more), each with a linkable anchor such as #ecdysis or #jacobsons-organ; DefinedTermSet JSON-LD

## Blog
- [SnakeWise blog](https://snakewise.org/blog/): species profiles and fact articles with cited, verified sources
- [How do egg-eating snakes eat eggs?](https://snakewise.org/blog/how-do-egg-eating-snakes-eat-eggs.html): African Dasypeltis (19 species) swallow bird eggs whole, crack them on downward spikes from vertebrae 17–38 and spit out the shell (Gartner & Greene 2008); adults can eat eggs of 98% of bird species (Barends & Maritz 2025), smaller heads than generalist rivals (Barends & Maritz 2021), egg preferences (Krupa & Slabach 2023), low feeding needs and seasonal eating (Barends & Maritz 2025), viper mimicry (Topper et al. 2026), origins of egg eating (de Queiroz & Rodríguez-Robles 2006) (2026-10-19)
- [Why do garter snakes form mating balls?](https://snakewise.org/blog/why-do-garter-snakes-form-mating-balls.html): red-sided garter snakes (Thamnophis sirtalis parietalis) at Manitoba's Narcisse Snake Dens; male-biased den sex ratios and females leaving within 3 days (Shine et al. 2004, Ecology and Society), up to 100 males per female (Manitoba Natural Resources), non-volatile methyl ketone female pheromone (Mason et al. 1989 Science), she-males (Mason & Crews 1985 Nature; Shine et al. 2000 Can J Zool) gaining warmth and predator cover (Shine et al. 2001 Nature), den mortality from crows and suffocation (Shine et al. 2001 Evolution), mating plugs (Shine et al. 2000 BJLS; Friesen et al. 2013 BJLS), Highway 17 tunnels (2026-10-20)
- [Study: dwarf reed snakes cartwheel to escape](https://snakewise.org/blog/dwarf-reed-snakes-cartwheel-escape-study.html): Kojima et al. 2026, Current Biology 36(20) R1061–R1063, doi:10.1016/j.cub.2026.08.057; three Pseudorabdion species from Kubah National Park, Sarawak, roll at 1.7–3.7 m/s with heads held steady, Calamaria relatives did not roll; first described in P. longiceps by Quah et al. 2023 (Biotropica, doi:10.1111/btp.13213).
- [Study: individual rattlesnakes are consistent in how much venom they use](https://snakewise.org/blog/rattlesnake-venom-personality-study.html): Martin & Hayes 2026, Frontiers in Ethology 5:1918065, doi:10.3389/fetho.2026.1918065; 48 southern Pacific rattlesnakes (Crotalus oreganus helleri), three venom extractions each; strikes, biting, venom pulses and venom volume all repeatable (R about 0.26–0.47; venom volume 0.41) after accounting for body size; larger snakes released more venom.
- [How venomous is the inland taipan?](https://snakewise.org/blog/how-venomous-is-the-inland-taipan.html): Oxyuranus microlepidotus, most toxic snake venom in mouse tests (LD50 ~0.01 mg/kg, ~17.3 mg per strike; Morrison et al. 1983), paradoxin neurotoxin (Hodgson et al. 2007), venom proteomics (Paz et al. 2025), juvenile vs adult venom (Tan et al. 1993), rare human bites and antivenom (Mirtschin et al. 1984; Weinstein et al. 2017, 2025), Australian snakebite deaths (Johnston et al. 2017), range and diet (Australian Museum) (2026-10-25)
- [Baby copperhead identification](https://snakewise.org/blog/baby-copperhead-identification.html): yellow tail tip used for caudal luring (Pisani & Riedle 2018; Royal Society Open Science 2022 fetal ultrasound), hourglass bands, plain head, copperhead vs corn snake table (UGA SREL; Missouri DOC); copperhead bite deaths rare, 5 of 101 US native snakebite deaths 1989–2018 (Greene et al. 2021; Parrish & Carr 1967; Walker & Morrison 2011; Seifert et al. 2009) (2026-10-26)
- [What is the longest snake in the world?](https://snakewise.org/blog/what-is-the-longest-snake-in-the-world.html): Malayopython reticulatus is the longest snake species; >4,200 harvested Sumatran pythons averaged 2.5–2.8 m SVL and 6–8 kg, ~1% over 4.5 m SVL, harvest stable over 20 years (Natusch et al. 2016); Agta python attacks and a 6.9 m python (Headland & Greene 2011); stretch bias in snake length (Rivas et al. 2008); Colossus corrected to 6.35 m (Barker et al. 2012; Foxon 2023); green anaconda heaviest, E. akayima split (Rivas et al. 2024; Smithsonian's National Zoo); Titanoboa ~13 m (Head et al. 2009; Rivas 2023) (2026-10-26)
- [Which snake has the longest fangs?](https://snakewise.org/blog/which-snake-has-the-longest-fangs.html): the Gaboon viper (Bitis gabonica), fangs up to about 5 cm (Smithsonian National Zoo; Guinness 50 mm in a 1.83 m snake) — how rotating viper fangs fold, why vipers evolved long fangs (Broeckhoven & du Plessis 2017; Cundall 2009), front-fang evolution (Jackson 2003; Vonk et al. 2008), ambush hunting and diet (Luiselli & Akani 2003), velvet-black camouflage (Spinner et al. 2013), bite risk (Marsh & Whaler 1984; Marsh et al. 2007) (2026-10-18)
- [What is the smallest snake in the world?](https://snakewise.org/blog/what-is-the-smallest-snake-in-the-world.html): the Barbados threadsnake (Tetracheilostoma carlae) — about 10 cm (max 104 mm), 0.60 g, a single long egg, why snakes cannot get much smaller (Hedges 2008), how threadsnakes eat ants, assessed as Critically Endangered (IUCN 2016), rediscovered March 2025 (2026-10-16)
- [Can snakes reproduce without mating?](https://snakewise.org/blog/can-snakes-reproduce-without-mating.html): Brahminy blind snake / flowerpot snake (Indotyphlops braminus) — only known obligate parthenogenetic snake; all-female, triploid (42 chromosomes), worldwide via potting soil (2026-10-12)
- [How do sidewinder snakes move?](https://snakewise.org/blog/how-do-sidewinders-move.html): how Crotalus cerastes sidewinds with two body waves, climbs sand dunes, turns, saves energy, and its special belly-scale texture (2026-10-09)
- [How long can a snake go without eating?](https://snakewise.org/blog/how-long-can-a-snake-go-without-eating.html): how snakes survive months of fasting (metabolism cut by up to 72%, fat burned while protein is spared) and how Burmese python guts and hearts grow after a meal and shrink back (2026-10-11)
- [How do king cobras build nests?](https://snakewise.org/blog/how-do-king-cobras-build-nests.html): female Ophiophagus hannah piles leaf litter into a mound nest about 3 °C warmer than air, guards the clutch, and leaves before hatching (2026-10-14)
- [How do sea snakes breathe through their skin?](https://snakewise.org/blog/how-do-sea-snakes-breathe-through-their-skin.html): yellow-bellied sea snake (Hydrophis platurus) cutaneous respiration — skin supplies up to 33% of resting O2 and releases most CO2; dives to 50 m for up to 213 min; still needs its lung and fresh rainwater (2026-10-15)
- [Can snakes hear?](https://snakewise.org/blog/can-snakes-hear.html): snakes have no ears or eardrums but hear low sounds and vibrations through the jaw, quadrate and columella to the inner ear; royal pythons most sensitive at 80 to 160 Hz, rattlesnakes respond to airborne 200 to 400 Hz tones, and Australian genera react differently to sound (2026-10-13)
- [Paradise flying snake: how a snake with no wings glides](https://snakewise.org/blog/paradise-flying-snake.html): range, size, diet, and how Chrysopelea paradisi jumps, flattens and undulates to glide (2026-10-08)

## Tools

## Games
- [SnakeWise games](https://snakewise.org/games/): hub of free, original snake games that teach real facts
- [Lookalike Lab](https://snakewise.org/games/lookalike-lab/): venomous or harmless quiz using clues from the ID guide (learning only, not safety advice)
- [Scale Snap](https://snakewise.org/games/scale-snap/): memory match of snake markings, each pair revealing which species wears it
- [Shed Shuffle](https://snakewise.org/games/shed-shuffle/): tile-swap picture puzzle about how snakes shed their skin

- [Privacy Policy](https://snakewise.org/privacy.html): no accounts or ad cookies; cookieless Cloudflare Web Analytics; contact form via FormSubmit; GitHub Pages logs, Google Fonts, local game scores
- [Disclaimer](https://snakewise.org/disclaimer.html): accuracy, snake ID and safety, advertising and affiliate (FTC) disclosure
- [Photo and asset credits](https://snakewise.org/credits/): author, source and licence (CC0, CC BY, public domain) for every photo; fonts; original artwork
- [Study: venomous snakes are more likely to stand out from their surroundings](https://snakewise.org/blog/venomous-snakes-stand-out-colour-study.html): news on Duclaux, Dugon & Healy 2026 (Journal of Animal Ecology, doi:10.1111/1365-2656.70351), 458 species, venomous snakes more contextually conspicuous; no link to venom potency or pain; colour alone is not a safe ID rule (2026-10-15)
- [Study: Sri Lanka's spectacled cobras form a distinct genetic lineage](https://snakewise.org/blog/sri-lankan-spectacled-cobras-distinct-lineage-study.html): news on Kanunjna, Sunagar et al. 2026 (Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution 223:108654, doi:10.1016/j.ympev.2026.108654), 67 cobras, nine markers; mainland Indian Naja naja largely panmictic; Sri Lankan lineage diverged ~2 million years ago, possibly via sea-level change; not declared a separate species (2026-10-16)
- [Study: snakes escalate their warning sounds before biting](https://snakewise.org/blog/snakes-escalate-warnings-before-biting-study.html): news on Van Zele, Lourdais et al. 2026 (Functional Ecology, doi:10.1111/1365-2435.70452), 220 snakes from 73 species, four sound modes (hissing, tail vibration, rattling, scale rubbing); warnings lengthen and intensify with threat, biting mostly at the highest threat level, larger snakes less likely to bite (2026-10-17)
- [Study: simple hygiene could stop people spreading snake fungal disease](https://snakewise.org/blog/snake-fungal-disease-australia-biosecurity-study.html): news on Champagne, Butcher, Bourke, Seneci & Grogan 2026 (Conservation Biology, doi:10.1111/cobi.70391), how reptile handlers could spread Ophidiomyces ophidiicola and other fungi, and their hygiene guidelines; background from Butcher et al. 2026 (Australian Veterinary Journal, doi:10.1111/avj.70060), first wild Australian cases
- [Study: removing large female Burmese pythons has the biggest impact](https://snakewise.org/blog/burmese-python-removal-index-large-females-study.html): news on Romer, Miller, Balaguera-Reina, Mazzotti et al. 2026 (Ecological Applications 36(6):e70317, doi:10.1002/eap.70317), the Weighted Removal Index for invasive Python bivittatus in South Florida, SFWMD Python Elimination Program data; neural network best (balanced accuracy 0.703); higher-impact surveys in waning moon phases and warm, humid weather (2026-10-19)
